title: Deer Lichen, Foraged Spices, and a Gold Medal: How Vancouver's Kavita Is Rewriting the Indian Restaurant Playbook
excerpt: Chef Tushar Tondvalkar's Konkan-coast-meets-Pacific-Northwest concept has swept Vancouver's 2026 restaurant awards, signalling a new era for Indian fine dining in North America.
body:
For decades, Indian restaurants in North America have operated within a familiar grammar: butter chicken, tikka masala, garlic naan, and a red-and-gold dining room. Chef Tushar Tondvalkar has torn up that script. His restaurant Kavita, tucked into Vancouver's Olympic Village neighbourhood, has just won Gold for Best Indian Restaurant at the prestigious 2026 Vancouver Magazine Restaurant Awards — and Silver for Best New Restaurant across all cuisines.

## From Malvan to the Pacific Northwest

Tondvalkar's culinary roots trace back to Mumbai and the coastal town of Malvan in Maharashtra, where he first learned to cook over charcoal fires with his family's matriarchs. But Kavita is no nostalgia project. The restaurant focuses on the regional flavours of the Konkan and Maharashtrian coasts — areas that most North American diners have never encountered on a menu — reimagined through hyper-local Pacific Northwest ingredients.

The tasting menu changes daily, dictated not by a recipe binder but by whatever proteins and produce arrive at the kitchen door. On any given evening, you might encounter a spiced chickpea purée served on a crisped bit of deer lichen, or eggplant paired with spiced yogurt and a startlingly bright orange-pine sorbet. Judges at the awards were unambiguous: "The cooking is off the charts," wrote one panelist.

## A Clean Sweep for Indian Cuisine

Kavita wasn't the only Indian restaurant honoured. Vikram Vij's legendary **Vij's** on Cambie Street — the restaurant that helped put Indian cuisine on Vancouver's culinary map over two decades ago — took Silver. Newcomer **Peya** in East Vancouver earned Bronze for its French-Indian fusion, including a rabbit kebab atop a bed of bright green pistou that has become an instant signature dish. Meanwhile, **Sula**, which specialises in elevated North Indian and Mangalorean seafood cuisine, won Bronze in the Best Chain category.

The message is clear: Indian cuisine is no longer a niche ethnic category in Canadian dining. It is competing at — and winning — the highest tiers of North American gastronomy.

## Why This Matters for the Diaspora

For the roughly 1.9 million Canadians of Indian origin and millions more across the United States, Kavita's success represents something deeper than a restaurant review. It is validation that Indian culinary traditions can anchor serious, chef-driven fine dining without diluting their identity.

Tondvalkar's approach — roasting and grinding whole spices in-house, foraging local ingredients, building a 1,500-square-foot open kitchen where guests watch every dish come together — is the kind of meticulous craft that earns Michelin stars in other cuisines. The fact that he does it with Konkan coastal flavours rather than the French or Nordic canon that typically dominates fine dining is a quiet revolution.

## What's Next

Kavita is already among the hardest reservations to land in Vancouver, regularly appearing as the most-booked Indian restaurant on OpenTable. Tondvalkar has spoken about eventually expanding the concept to other cities, but for now, the focus remains on the daily tasting menu and the relationships with local foragers and fishers that define the restaurant's identity.

For Indian chefs across North America watching from their own kitchens, the takeaway is simple: the days of Indian cuisine being boxed into a buffet or a budget takeaway category are over. The gold medal says so.
author: Diaspora Desk
